act1.left: …at the instant t0=0, when the curtain opens!
…if it is S.H.M., then the values we measure must satisfy x=A·sin(ωt+φ₀)!
…if we draw the x–t graph, it can confirm it!
…and since x₀={x0} m is not zero, there is also an initial phase φ₀={phi0}°. Haha, one thing to keep in mind!
…therefore the velocity is given by the law v=ωA·cos(ωt+φ₀)!
But the relation x=A·sin(ωt+φ₀) (1) is contained in (3): a = -ω²A·sin(ωt+φ₀) = -ω²x! So the new law is written as a(x)= -ω²x
Perfect! The whole set of S.H.M. laws!
Hmm...What remains is to see how it actually manages to perform S.H.M.!

act2.left: Oops! This m₁D₁ is attached to a spring!
I've seen this exact same m1D₁ before with the same spring mechanism in another play, but there it had a different producer!
...yes, and there again it kept moving obsessively with the same period, but with a larger amplitude A!
What's the point of digging into that? Let's see exactly what it's doing here!
Hmm… the real protagonist is probably the moving actor together with their tools!
Now I think I understand why they don't just call it m₁, but m₁,D₁!…
…m₁ is the mass of the actor, but the oscillator is clearly the combination of the actor (m₁) and the elastic cause–force that D₁ seems to refer to!
…so m₁ and D₁ always come as a package! and the two together are the oscillator – the protagonist!

…so every oscillator is characterized by
1. its mass, and
2. the elastic cause–force, which sets the period T of its oscillation!
…I'm starting to be convinced why its characteristic name is m D and not just m!...

So the peculiarity of each oscillator – its “obsession” with having its own characteristic period T (and therefore characteristic f and ω) – is due to 1. its “body type” m, and 2. the elastic cause (which is probably encoded in the D in its name)!
Wooow! come on guys! leave it, let's move on…!
Alright then! Let's see how Newton's 2nd Law is written for the oscillator's case.
…uhm, ΣF = m·a in general, and so here, using (3), ΣF = −mω²A·sin(ωt+φ₀) (5)!
…and using (4) it can also be written as ΣF = −mω²x (6)!
However! Equation (6) – look at it – contains two constants of the actor: their “body type” (m) and their “obsession” (ω)!
What if we bundle those two constants into one and call it D = mω² (6’)? Does that make sense?

So, if we assign this new constant to the elastic cause as its own constant D, then everything makes sense:
1. the actor has their own fixed mass m₁,
2. the elastic cause has its own constant D₁...
... That way, it’s explained why the actor, regardless of stage and producer, “obsessively” keeps their period constant?
...Exactly! (6’) D = mω² shows it: if m and D are fixed, then ω=√(D/m) is also fixed for the actor!
…hmm, so it's justified that the protagonist–oscillator (=actor + elastic cause) is called (m,D)!
…but also equation (6) – let's not forget! – becomes ΣF = −D·x (7)!
